title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Why one more township hit the brakes and what it means for power, water and your bills.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're talking about the growing wave of local pauses on these massive projects and what it could mean for electric rates, water supplies, and communities across the state.
Yesterday Pere Marquette Township in Mason County enacted a one-year moratorium on new data center permitting and construction.
That's the second or third one we've heard about this week. What's driving these decisions, Graham?
The board cited concerns over energy and water demands. They adopted ordinances that temporarily ban new projects, and it could be extended.
So this isn't just one isolated vote. How does this fit into the bigger picture of what's happening around Michigan?
It's part of a pattern. Manistee Township also halted new proposals yesterday, aligning with nearby townships. East Lansing extended its own freeze while staff writes rules on power use and setbacks.
And these aren't small places. What are the real stakes for residents who might live 30 or 40 miles away?

That's the key point. Data centers can pull millions of gallons of water daily for cooling and require enormous amounts of power. If they connect to the same grid, ratepayers across the region can see indirect hikes even if the facility isn't in their backyard.
We've also got new state rules tightening Great Lakes water withdrawals that were posted today. How does that layer on top of these local moves?

Exactly. The new diversion tracking directly limits how much large cooling operations can take from the basin. Projects under discussion in several counties would need those volumes, so the state rules become a hard cap on future builds.

And then there's the Cass County town hall today where Save Cass County packed the room with neighbors worried about noise, water, and rising bills. They're pushing officials to reject or restrict projects before more land gets optioned.
Right, and that meeting was standing-room only. It shows the grassroots pressure building in multiple counties at once.
So when a township like Pere Marquette puts in a full year pause, what happens next? Can they extend it or turn it permanent?

The ordinance allows for possible extension, and many places are using the time to write permanent zoning rules on noise, setbacks, and utility strain. Coldwater is holding a joint meeting Monday to gather feedback on exactly that.
What about the power side? We saw DTE scouting a Milan Township site for a new gas plant aimed at serving these big loads. Does that change the equation?

It shows how the scramble is rippling out. A new gas plant would bring its own air-quality and rate impacts, and residents 30 miles away could feel both the higher bills and the infrastructure changes.
There's also that legal challenge in Saline Township over a tax abatement that an attorney says bypassed required steps. Could that delay projects even where approvals have already happened?

Yes, the challenge claims the township didn't follow proper procedures, which could shift millions in taxes away from local services and schools. Nearby residents are watching how it affects their property taxes.
And Coldwater area townships held their first public briefing yesterday on proposed centers, covering power needs, water use, and tax impacts before any formal applications.
That's the proactive approach some places are taking — getting the details out early so residents can weigh in before land is locked up.
How many townships are now in some form of pause or review mode? It feels like it's spreading quickly.

At least half a dozen we've tracked in the last week alone, from Mason and Manistee to East Lansing and now Coldwater looking at permanent rules. The common thread is protecting farmland, water, and keeping utility rates stable for existing residents.
What should listeners 30 or 60 miles from any of these sites be watching for in the coming weeks?
The Monday meetings in Coldwater and Kalamazoo, plus Caledonia Township's planning commission session on ordinance changes. Those are the next places where rules could get locked in.
And if more townships follow Pere Marquette's lead with a full year pause, does that slow the overall buildout or just push developers to other counties?
It creates breathing room for communities to set their own terms. Developers may look for friendlier spots, but the state water rules and grid constraints are statewide limits that apply everywhere.
So the moratorium isn't the end of the story — it's the start of a longer zoning fight in many places.
That's right. The one-year clock gives time to study the real impacts on power and water before any permits move forward.
And with the new Great Lakes diversion tracking in place, some of those water-heavy proposals may simply not pencil out.
Exactly. The combination of local pauses and tighter state water rules is reshaping where and whether these projects can proceed.
Listeners should keep an eye on how the Coldwater Monday meeting plays out — it could set a template for other townships.
We'll have the details on that and more tomorrow. Let's move to quick hits on the other stories from the last day.
Starting with today's Cass County town hall — Save Cass County drew a huge crowd pushing officials to block or restrict data centers over noise, water, and electric bills.
And 30 miles away, residents could still see rate impacts if those sites tie into the same grid.
Also today, Michigan posted new tracking on Great Lakes water diversions that will limit how much data centers can pull for cooling.
That's a direct limit on the millions of gallons daily that several proposed facilities would need.
Yesterday in Branch County, Coldwater area townships held their first public briefing on proposed centers, covering power, water, and tax impacts.
And Coldwater is also prepping permanent zoning rules to shield neighborhoods from noise and utility strain, with a Monday feedback session.
Manistee Township joined the pause yesterday, blocking large-scale projects that would draw heavy power and water.
Nearby communities now face the same questions about future growth and rates.
In Saline Township, a tax break for a data center is facing a legal challenge over whether proper steps were followed.
That could delay or derail the deal and affect local services and school funding.
DTE is eyeing a Milan Township site for a new gas plant to serve data-center demand.
Residents 30 miles away would feel it through higher rates and air-quality considerations if approved.
And East Lansing extended its moratorium yesterday so staff can finish rules on power use and setbacks.
That gives surrounding townships a model to watch for their own zoning fights.
Now let's look ahead to the meetings listeners can actually attend.
Monday, August 17, Coldwater City Council, Planning Commission, and Board of Public Utilities are holding a joint informational meeting on data center impacts, zoning, and regulation options.
Same day, the City of Coldwater Planning Commission and CBPU Board will discuss zoning and regulation of high-utility data centers.
Caledonia Township Planning Commission meets Monday for a data center ordinance discussion and potential zoning amendments.
And Kalamazoo City Commission will vote Monday on a resolution for a temporary moratorium on data center development.
Those are the sessions where residents can show up and weigh in before rules get finalized.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Pere Marquette's Year-Long Pause Signals Wider Michigan Pushback on Data Centers
